nodes.title: Glycaemic Control in Critical Illness
nodes.summary: This section reviews glycaemic control in critical illness, covering glucose targets, insulin delivery protocols, and monitoring frequency. It also addresses hypoglycemia management, confounding factors like steroids, and current research limitations.

children.title: Glycaemic Control in Critical Illness — Overview
children.summary: This document is a synthetic test document intended for system testing and indexing, not clinical guidance. It presents plausible content structured as a preprint regarding glycaemic control in critical illness.
children.content:
> **SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT — NOT CLINICAL GUIDANCE.** Written to exercise the
> ingest, indexing and retrieval pipeline. The recommendations below are
> plausible in shape but must never be used for patient care. Presented in the
> shape of a preprint to exercise a nested source folder.

children.title: Abstract
children.summary: This review summarizes current targets for stress hyperglycemia in critically ill adults, noting its association with mortality. It discusses individualizing glucose control based on diabetes status and necessary monitoring.
children.content:
Stress hyperglycaemia is present in roughly half of critically ill adults and is
associated with mortality independently of pre-existing diabetes. Trials of tight
control have repeatedly shown that the harm of hypoglycaemia offsets the benefit
of lower mean glucose. This review summarises current targets, the case for
individualising them by diabetes status, and the monitoring required to make any
target safe.

children.title: Targets
children.summary: This section outlines blood glucose targets for critically ill adults generally and specifically addresses adjustments needed for patients with pre-existing diabetes, detailing appropriate target ranges based on individual risk factors.

children.title: The General Target
children.summary: The passage specifies a general blood glucose target of 8–10 mmol/L for critically ill adults and advises starting insulin when glucose exceeds 10 mmol/L twice. It warns against tight control to 4.5–6.0 mmol/L due to increased hypoglycemia risk.
children.content:
Target a blood glucose of 8–10 mmol/L for most critically ill adults. Start
insulin when glucose exceeds 10 mmol/L on two consecutive readings.

Tight control to 4.5–6.0 mmol/L increases severe hypoglycaemia roughly six-fold
and increases mortality. It should not be used outside a trial protocol.

children.title: Patients with Pre-existing Diabetes
children.summary: The passage discusses glycemic control targets for patients with pre-existing diabetes, noting that those with HbA1c above 64 mmol/mol may need a higher glucose range of 10–14 mmol/L and recommends measuring admission HbA1c.
children.content:
Patients with a pre-admission HbA1c above 64 mmol/mol tolerate — and may
require — a higher range of 10–14 mmol/L. Rapid normalisation in a chronically
hyperglycaemic patient produces relative hypoglycaemia at glucose values that
would be unremarkable in anyone else.

Measure HbA1c on admission in every patient with hyperglycaemia. It distinguishes
stress hyperglycaemia from undiagnosed diabetes and sets the appropriate target
for the admission.

children.title: Insulin Delivery
children.summary: This section covers insulin delivery protocols in critical illness, detailing when to use continuous intravenous infusion versus subcutaneous routes based on hemodynamic stability. It also provides guidelines for managing hypoglycemia following interruptions to enteral nutrition.

children.title: Route
children.summary: The passage advises using continuous intravenous insulin infusion for hemodynamically unstable patients or those on vasopressors due to unreliable subcutaneous absorption in shock. Transitioning to subcutaneous insulin requires stable eating and cessation of vasopressors.
children.content:
Use a continuous intravenous infusion while the patient is haemodynamically
unstable or receiving vasopressors. Subcutaneous absorption is unreliable in
shock, and apparent insulin resistance is frequently a perfusion problem rather
than a dosing one.

Transition to subcutaneous insulin only once the patient is eating and
vasopressors have been stopped. Overlap the infusion with the first subcutaneous
dose by 2 hours, since intravenous insulin has a half-life of minutes.

children.title: Nutrition Interruptions
children.summary: The passage addresses hypoglycaemia in intensive care, specifically caused by continuing insulin infusion after an interrupted enteral feed. It advises reviewing the insulin protocol as a mandatory checklist item during any feed interruption.
children.content:
The commonest cause of hypoglycaemia in intensive care is an insulin infusion
continuing after enteral feed has been interrupted for a procedure. The insulin
protocol must be reviewed at every feed interruption, and this should be a
checklist item rather than a matter of memory.

children.title: Monitoring
children.summary: This passage details glucose monitoring frequency in critical illness, specifying hourly checks until stable for four hours, then every two hours. It advises using arterial or venous blood gas glucose when vasopressors are used and notes limitations of point-of-care testing.
children.content:
Measure hourly until glucose is within range for 4 consecutive hours, then every
2 hours. Return to hourly after any rate change, any change in nutrition, or the
initiation of corticosteroids.

Point-of-care capillary testing is unreliable in shock, oedema and anaemia. Use
arterial or venous blood gas glucose in any patient on vasopressors.

Continuous glucose monitoring shows promise in this population but is not yet
validated for insulin dosing during vasopressor therapy.

children.title: Hypoglycaemia
children.summary: The passage details immediate treatment for glucose below 4.0 mmol/L using 100 mL of 20% glucose intravenously and mandates recording episodes below 3.0 mmol/L as safety incidents due to associated mortality risks.
children.content:
Treat any glucose below 4.0 mmol/L immediately with 100 mL of 20% glucose
intravenously, then recheck after 15 minutes. Do not simply reduce the infusion
rate and wait.

Record every episode below 3.0 mmol/L as a patient safety incident. Severe
hypoglycaemia in critical illness carries an association with mortality
comparable to that of severe hyperglycaemia, and episodes cluster around
identifiable process failures rather than being distributed at random.

children.title: Steroids and Other Confounders
children.summary: The passage discusses how corticosteroids like prednisolone predictably raise glucose levels, peaking 4–8 hours post-dose. It also notes that continuous renal replacement therapy with glucose-containing fluid adds an unrecognised glucose load.
children.content:
Corticosteroids raise glucose predictably, with the peak effect 4–8 hours after
a morning dose of prednisolone. Anticipate the rise rather than reacting to it.

Continuous renal replacement therapy with glucose-containing replacement fluid
adds a variable and frequently unrecognised glucose load.

children.title: Research Gaps
children.summary: The passage notes a lack of prospective trials comparing HbA1c-stratified targets to fixed targets for glycaemic control in critical illness. Current recommendations rely on observational data and physiological reasoning.
children.content:
No trial has yet tested an HbA1c-stratified target prospectively against a fixed
target. Until one does, the recommendation to individualise by diabetes status
rests on observational data and physiological reasoning.
